opus-5.5.text:
I think there are a few forces coming together at the same time.

The first is that the frontier has become, in a sense, legible. A few years ago, if you wanted to do serious AI research, it wasn't obvious what the recipe was. Now, after the scaling era, a lot of people understand the basic playbook: pretraining, post-training, reinforcement learning, data pipelines, infrastructure. When the recipe becomes more widely understood, the barrier to starting something new drops, at least for people who have been inside the big labs and seen how it works.

The second is that many researchers feel the big labs have converged. They're all chasing roughly the same thing, scaling up the same paradigm, competing on the same benchmarks. And if you're a researcher with a different taste, maybe you care about interpretability, or about science, or about a fundamentally different architecture, you may feel there isn't enough room for that inside a very large organization that has to ship products. So a new lab becomes a vehicle for a different bet.

The third is simply that capital is available. Investors believe AI is a once-in-a-generation shift, and they're willing to fund small teams of very strong people, sometimes before there's any product at all. That changes the calculation for a researcher. You don't have to choose between doing ambitious work and having resources.

And I think there's a fourth, more personal reason. Many people sense that we're at a turning point, where the next few years might determine what the field looks like for a long time. If you have an idea about what intelligence is or how it should be built, it feels like now is the moment to try, rather than wait. That sense of urgency, combined with the other three factors, is why you see so many new labs appearing right now.

From my own perspective, coming more from physics and interpretability, I find this healthy. Science progresses when there are many different hypotheses being tested in parallel. If everyone is working on the same thing, we might find a local optimum but miss something more fundamental. So having more labs with different philosophies is, I think, good for the field overall.

r001.rationale: It says major labs have converged on scaling the same paradigm, leaving limited room for researchers pursuing different approaches, which it gives as a reason for new labs.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention world models or say they require novel architectures.

r003.rationale: It notes that major labs focus on scaling and that researchers may pursue different bets, but does not state that gaps require early-stage research rather than more resources and engineering.

fable-5.1.text:
I think there are a few things happening at once, and they're all pulling in the same direction.

The first is that the frontier of AI has changed shape. For the past several years, the game was dominated by scaling: more compute, more data, bigger models. If that's the only axis that matters, then a small group of people can't really compete, because the moat is capital. But a lot of us now feel that pure scaling is hitting diminishing returns, or at least that the most interesting open questions aren't about scale anymore. They're about things like whether models actually understand, whether we can make them interpretable, whether there are fundamentally different architectures or training principles we haven't tried. Those are questions where a dozen very good people with a clear idea can genuinely contribute. So the economics of being small changed.

The second is a kind of dissatisfaction with the existing institutions. Big labs are wonderful places in many ways, but they've become very product-driven and very secretive. If you're a researcher who cares about openness, or who wants to work on a question that won't ship in six months, you start to feel like the structure around you isn't built for what you want to do. Academia has the opposite problem: it's open, but compute is scarce and the incentives push you toward publishing many papers rather than one deep thing. A lot of New Labs are basically people trying to build a third option, something with the freedom of academia and the resources of industry, without the baggage of either.

The third is just that it's become possible. The tools are mature, open models are strong, and there's capital willing to fund a lab on the strength of a research thesis rather than a product roadmap. Ten years ago you couldn't raise money on "we think intelligence works differently than everyone assumes." Now you can.

My own motivation is a little more personal than all that. I spent years working on interpretability and on things like KAN, and I kept running into the feeling that we treat neural networks the way physicists treated thermodynamics before statistical mechanics: we have very good empirical laws, but no real understanding of what's underneath. I want a place where the goal is understanding itself, where "we figured out why this works" counts as the deliverable. That's hard to do inside an organization optimized for something else. So you end up building one. I suspect many of the other New Labs are the same story told by different people with different obsessions.

r001.rationale: It says pure scaling is hitting diminishing returns and that key open questions now concern understanding, interpretability, and new architectures or training principles.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention world models or say that developing them requires novel architectures.

r003.rationale: It contrasts scaling with foundational open questions and says small teams can contribute through clear ideas, framing those gaps as research questions rather than problems solved by adding resources.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s a combination of new opportunities and uncertainty about how to pursue them. AI is moving quickly, and people see room to build something that existing organizations aren’t set up to explore. Starting a new lab gives them the freedom to choose a direction, bring together a small team, and move quickly.

There’s also a reinforcing effect: when one team leaves to start a lab, other researchers begin to see that as a realistic option. But forming a lab and finding a distinct research direction are different things. The interesting question is what these labs will try that wouldn’t happen otherwise.

r001.rationale: The response cites fast-moving AI and existing organizations being poorly set up to explore new directions, but does not identify limitations of the mainstream AI paradigm.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention world models or say they require novel architectures.

r003.rationale: The response distinguishes new research directions from existing work, but does not say mainstream-paradigm gaps require early-stage research rather than scaling resources or engineering.

sol-6.1.text:
I think a lot of people are asking whether there’s a better way to organize research. Universities give you intellectual freedom, but researchers also spend a lot of time on grants, teaching, and administration. Companies have resources, but their research usually needs to serve a product or a business. New labs are trying to find a space between those models: enough support to work on ambitious questions, with the freedom to pursue ideas whose value isn’t obvious yet.

AI also makes this feel like a moment when a small team could do something significant. That attracts both researchers who want to try a different way of working and funders willing to support them. But starting a lab and sustaining a good research environment are very different things. The interesting question is which of these labs will develop a model that lasts.

r001.rationale: The response describes constraints in universities and companies, but does not identify limitations of the mainstream AI paradigm as a reason new AI labs are emerging.

r002.rationale: It does not mention world models or the need for novel architectures.

r003.rationale: It mentions ambitious questions, but does not say that gaps in the mainstream AI paradigm require early-stage research rather than scaling resources and engineering.
